pages.name: Spin it up
pages.text: The [[net torque]] is the motor's torque less what the load and friction take. Here it is a steady 50 N m. Watch the speed line. It is straight. The speed gains the same 25 rad/s every second, so it reaches 151.8 rad/s in 6.1 s. A steady net torque gives a steady rise in speed, not a steady speed. The graph shows a straight speed line up to 151.8 rad/s.

pages.name: Steady torque
pages.task: A steady net torque of 50 N m spins the rig up from rest. What does its speed do?
pages.answer: It rises by the same amount every second
pages.why: The speed rises by the net torque ÷ I each second. Here that is 50 ÷ 2 = 25 rad/s every second. It keeps rising like this for as long as the torque acts. A real drive levels off only because its load takes more torque as it speeds up.

pages.name: Mass further out
pages.text: Why does a shaft with its mass further out spin up more slowly? Picture a shaft with just one arm. The arm pushes its mass round its circle with a force of the torque ÷ r. Here the mass slides from 0.2 m out to 0.4 m. The push halves. The mass must also go twice as fast round its bigger circle for the same shaft speed. So the radius counts twice. Each mass adds its mass × r² to the shaft's [[moment of inertia]], I.

pages.name: Moment of inertia
pages.task: Each 25 kg mass on the rig slides from 0.2 m out to 0.4 m. What is the rig's moment of inertia now?
pages.why: Each mass adds its mass × r² = 25 × 0.4² = 4 kg m². Two masses make 8 kg m². That is four times the 2 kg m² at 0.2 m, because the radius doubled and is squared.

pages.name: Two rigs
pages.text: Two rigs get the same 50 N m. On the left the masses sit 0.2 m out, so I is 2 kg m². On the right they sit 0.4 m out, so I is 8 kg m², four times as much. Both start from rest together. Both speed lines are straight. The right one climbs a quarter as steeply. So its run-up takes four times as long, 24.3 s against 6.1 s. Twice the radius means four times the run-up.

pages.name: Torque and power
pages.text: Power works the same way as for a winch. Picture a shaft with just one arm. The arm pushes its mass with the torque ÷ r. In one radian of turn, the mass moves r metres along its circle. So each radian, the torque does (T ÷ r) × r = T joules of work. The radius cancels out. The shaft turns ω radians each second. So the [[power]] is T × ω watts, with ω in rad/s. An 11 kW motor at 151.8 rad/s gives 11,000 ÷ 151.8 = 72.4 N m.

pages.name: Stored energy
pages.text: A spinning shaft stores energy. Each mass moves round its circle at ω × r. Its energy of motion is half its mass × that speed squared. Add both masses and the rig stores ½ × I × ω². The speed line is straight. The [[stored energy]] climbs as a curve, slowly at first and steeply at the end. That is because it goes with the speed squared. At 151.8 rad/s the rig holds 23.1 kJ. Masses further out store more energy at the same speed.

pages.name: Motor and pump
pages.text: A real motor's torque changes with its speed. A pump needs more torque the faster it turns. The [[net torque]] is the gap between their curves. It widens at first, as the motor nears its peak. Then it closes fast near full speed. So the speed line climbs faster and faster at first, then bends over. It levels off where the curves meet, near 1450 rev/min. There the motor's torque just matches the pump's. With a steady torque instead, the speed line would stay straight.
pages.alt: A motor spins a shaft with two 25 kilogram masses 0.2 metres out, driving a pump, with the motor and pump torque curves, and a graph of its speed against time.

pages.name: Where it settles
pages.task: A motor drives a pump from rest. Where does the shaft's speed stop rising?
pages.answer: Where the motor and pump curves meet
pages.why: The speed keeps rising while there is any net torque. The net torque is the gap between the curves. It shrinks to nothing where they meet, near 1450 rev/min. There the speed holds steady.

pages.task: A rig has two 10 kg masses 0.3 m out. A steady net torque of 30 N m spins it up from rest. How long does it take to reach 600 rev/min?
pages.why: I = 2 × 10 × 0.3² = 1.8 kg m². So the speed rises 30 ÷ 1.8 = 16.7 rad/s each second. 600 rev/min is 62.8 rad/s. So the run-up takes 62.8 ÷ 16.7 = 3.8 s.

pages.name: Steady running
pages.task: A pump shaft runs at a steady 1450 rev/min. Its motor gives 72.4 N m. What is the net torque on the shaft?
pages.why: The speed is steady, so it is not rising. So the net torque must be zero. The pump takes all 72.4 N m that the motor gives: 72.4 − 72.4 = 0 N m.
